item.title: When the future loses its voice | Science
item.description: Across many high-income societies, anxiety about demographic decline has become commonplace. Fertility rates have fallen below replacement level, populations are aging rapidly, and governments worry about labor shortages, pension sustainability, and the future of welfare systems. These concerns are legitimate. Yet the conventional narrative does not always capture another important consequence of declining birth rates: dejuvenation, the progressive reduction of the demographic, economic, cultural and political weight of younger generations in society. Although low fertility alone does not immediately transform institutions, the cumulative effect of decades of low births combined with rising longevity does. The result is a thinner presence of younger people in the labor market, in entrepreneurship and innovation, and in the democratic debates in which long-term priorities are contested.

item.title: Editor’s Note for the Report “Host genetic diversity enables Ebola hemorrhagic fever pathogenesis and resistance” | Science
item.description: On 30 October 2014, Science published the Report “Host genetic diversity enables Ebola hemorrhagic fever pathogenesis and resistance” by A. L. Rasmussen et al. (1). The authors were recently made aware that figs. S3, S5, and S6 were published with incorrect images. In fig. S3, images of resistant mock-infected spleen (fig. S3C) and liver (fig. S3O) on day 3 after infection were inadvertently prepared from the same source image. Original data are not available to correct the figure. Higher-magnification images from the same conditions remain in the supplemental materials, with fig. S3D showing spleen and fig. S3P showing liver. In figs. S5 and S6, panels C, D, F, G, H, K, L, N, O, and P were inadvertently prepared from the same source images and duplicated in both figures. Original data are not available to correct the figures. The conclusion that there are similar levels of inflammation in spleen and liver remains supported by data in fig. S4 but is weakened by removing the corroborating data in fig. S5. Science is posting this Editor’s Note to alert readers to these issues. We are not taking further action because the main conclusions of the paper remain supported.
